top_story: Trump’s threat on 23 March to destroy Iran’s power infrastructure if Tehran did not reopen the Strait of Hormuz pushed Iranian leaders toward explicit warnings of wider regional escalation, sharpening the coercive backdrop for every active front. In Lebanon, a US-brokered ceasefire has now evolved into a more ambitious diplomatic opening, with President Joseph Aoun framing White House-backed talks with Israel as a bid for “permanent agreements” after Trump said Israel accepted a 10-day halt in fighting. That contrast between de-escalation on the Lebanese front and rising pressure on Iran unfolds alongside the entrenched violence of Israel’s detention regime, where the arrest and abuse of more than 700 Palestinian women and girls since the Gaza war began underscores that humanitarian harm remains a baseline condition rather than a byproduct of diplomacy. The regional picture is one of selective stabilization layered over deeper coercion, leaving fragile political openings vulnerable to being overtaken by unresolved Israeli-Palestinian violence and a widening US-Iran confrontation.
